Grade 2 · Unit 2-A

Materials and Their Uses

How do we choose and change materials to make useful things?

Everything we use is made of something, and the choice of material matters. You will sort materials by what they are like, pick the best one for a job, take objects apart and rebuild them from the same pieces, and find out which changes from heating and cooling can be undone and which cannot.

In this lesson

  1. Materials have properties we can observe
  2. We choose materials for jobs
  3. Pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt
  4. Heating and cooling can change materials
  5. Try it at home
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Rainproof Note

You did this before / what is new. You did fair tests in Unit 0 or K2.0; now you use a fair test to choose the best material for a real job.

Look for the tags AnalogyDiagramTry itDataReal world

Concept 1

Materials have properties we can observe

We can sort materials by things like hardness, softness, flexibility, and whether they keep water out.

Analogy

A closet with rain boots, mittens, and paper.

“Rubber keeps water out. Paper gets wet.”

Try it

Sort objects into hard/soft, bendy/stiff, waterproof/not waterproof.

“Put all hard things here.”

Data

Class property chart.

“5 things are waterproof. 3 are not.”

Concept 2

We choose materials for jobs

The best material depends on what we need it to do.

Try it

Spray water on paper, foil, cloth, and plastic wrap to see which keeps a paper note dry.

“Which one keeps the note dry?”

Data

Table with dry/wet results.

“Foil: dry. Cloth: wet.”

Real world

Raincoats and bike helmets.

“A raincoat keeps water out. A helmet is hard outside.”

Concept 3

Pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt

Many objects are made of pieces, and the same pieces can make a new object.

Try it

Take apart a small block tower, bead strand, or paper-chain, then rebuild a new shape.

“Take it apart. Make something new.”

Diagram

Same pieces shown before and after.

“Same pieces. New shape.”

Real world

A block or building-toy set.

“The same blocks can build a car or a house.”

Concept 4

Heating and cooling can change materials

Some changes caused by warming or cooling can be undone, and some cannot.

Analogy

Some changes have an “undo,” and some do not.

“Some changes can undo. Some cannot.”

Try it

Watch ice melt into water, then refreeze if possible. Adult may use warm water. Compare with a photo or teacher demo of a cooked egg and toast.

“Ice becomes water. Water can become ice again.”

Data

Argument table: “Can it change back?” with evidence.

“Can it change back? What is your evidence?”

Real world

Michigan snow melts and can freeze again.

“Snow melts. Puddles can freeze.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Rainproof Note. Problem: a paper note must stay dry. Students sketch, choose two materials, test each with 3 sprays of water, record dry/wet, and choose the best material using evidence. Criteria: the note stays dry, and the cover bends around the note. If two materials both stay dry, the second criterion decides. Constraints: use kit materials and keep the test fair (same number of sprays, same distance).

Try it

What you need

assorted safe objects (wood, plastic, metal, fabric, paper, rubber), tray, paper notes, spray bottle, foil, cloth, plastic wrap, blocks/beads/paper chain, ice cube, small cup, butter or crayon wax, picture cards for cooked egg/toast, paper, crayons.

Safety: Adult handles warm things. No tasting. Wash hands after handling materials, especially food items. No coin cells or magnets are required.

Try it

What you do

Sort materials, run the Rainproof Note fair test, take apart and rebuild pieces, observe ice/butter changes, and construct an argument about reversible and irreversible changes.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

Real observation log is preferred; this dataset guarantees evidence for 2-PS1-4 if you cannot melt/refreeze live. | Change | Before | After | Can it change back? | Evidence sentence | |---|---|---|---|---| | Ice cube | Solid ice | Water | Yes | The water froze back into ice. | | Butter | Solid butter | Melted butter | Yes | It hardened again when cooled. | | Egg | Raw egg | Cooked egg | No | It stayed solid after cooling. | | Bread | Soft bread | Toast | No | It did not become bread again. | Optional Rainproof Note backup data: | Material | Try 1 | Try 2 | Try 3 | Result | |---|---|---|---|---| | Plastic wrap | Dry | Dry | Dry | Meets the goal | | Foil | Dry | Dry | Dry | Meets the goal | | Cloth | Damp | Wet | Wet | Not good | | Paper | Wet | Wet | Wet | Not good |

Near you: Michigan materials include copper, iron, salt, sand, wood, and water. Winter ice and snow show heating/cooling changes. Child text: “Michigan has metal, wood, water, and ice.”

Words to know

material
what something is made of.
property
something we can observe about it.
waterproof
keeps water out.
flexible
bends without breaking.
pieces
small parts that can make a whole.
melt
solid becomes liquid.
freeze
liquid becomes solid.
reversible
can change back.
irreversible
cannot change back.
evidence
what we observe that helps answer.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “We sort materials only by size.” Correct: we sort by properties such as hard, soft, bendy, waterproof.
  • “All changes can be undone.” Correct: some changes can be reversed; some cannot.
  • “Only water can melt and freeze.” Correct: other materials, like butter, can melt and harden with safe warming and cooling.
  • “Heating only makes things feel warm.” Correct: heating can melt or soften; cooling can harden or freeze.
  • “A material’s job is the same as its property.” Correct: a property describes the material; a job is how we use it.

Limits and cautions:

  • Heating/cooling must stay safe: use ice, room temperature, sunlight, or adult-handled warm water only. Adult handles warm things.
  • If you cannot refreeze live, the provided dataset can still support an evidence-based argument, but live observation is stronger.
  • 2-PS1-3 works best with blocks, beads, or paper chains; avoid glued objects.
  • Food materials are for observing only; no tasting.
  • If a teacher adds a light or magnet extension, use ready-made lamps only and keep magnets away from Chromebooks.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 2-PS1-1: Plan and conduct an investigation to gather data to classify materials by observable properties.
  • 2-PS1-2: Analyze data from testing materials to choose the best material for a purpose.
  • 2-PS1-3: Make observations to determine how an object made of small pieces can be taken apart and made into something new.
  • 2-PS1-4: Construct an argument with evidence that some changes caused by heating or cooling can be reversed and some cannot.

Connections: - Builds on: K2.0 *Science Noticing and Asking* (optional), K-A *Pushes and Pulls*, 1-A *Sound and Light*. - Builds toward: 5.1 *Matter, Mixtures, and Changes*; 4.5 *Earth’s Surface: Rocks, Maps, Erosion, Resources*; Unit 2: *Thermal Energy*; Unit 10: *States of Matter*; 7.1 *Structure & Properties of Matter*; 7.2 *Chemical Reactions & Matter*.
